transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Tensorlytics x Redwood — Dedicated customer performance review (latency variance + canary updates)
Date: 2026-01-22
Time: 9:00 AM PT
Duration: 53 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Marissa Cole, Aisha Bello, Noah Patel, Vanessa Ortiz
Tensorlytics: Lena Park, Derek Morrow, Priya Nair

Auto-summary (generated)
- Tensorlytics reported noticeable p95 latency variance in eu-west dedicated over the last ~10 days, mostly affecting tail latency during peak hours.
- Redwood reviewed early indicators pointing to queueing-time increases + batch size distribution shifts, likely tied to a fleet/SKU mix change and a scheduling heuristic update.
- Redwood shared updates on the new always-on performance canary that has been catching regressions earlier and improving rollback speed; Tensorlytics requested canary signals be shared (warning-level) for their dedicated pool.
- Agreed next steps: Redwood to send detailed breakdown and correlate with fleet changes; Redwood to enable warning alerts (non-paging) and share dashboards; Tensorlytics to share top request shapes for SLO alignment.

Topics
1) What changed: where the variance showed up (eu-west, peak, tail)
2) Breakdown: prefill vs decode vs queueing; batch size distribution
3) Canary update: detection, false positives, rollout gating
4) Actions: alerting thresholds, reporting, follow-up cadence

Action items (as discussed)
- Redwood: provide a 14-day perf report and correlate with infra changes
- Redwood: enable canary warning-level signals for Tensorlytics model in eu-west
- Tensorlytics: share top request shapes and “what matters” SLO language

Transcript

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Alright, cool. I think we’re all here. Lena, Derek, Priya — good to see you. This is the dedicated performance review. We wanted to spend most of the time on the eu-west latency variance you flagged and then give a quick update on the regression canary improvements we’ve been rolling out.

[00:18] Lena Park: Yep, thanks Marissa. This has been a bit of a fire drill on our side. Not like full outage, but enough tail pain that support tickets start showing up.

[00:29] Marissa Cole: Totally understood. Aisha’s here from SRE/SLO side, Noah from runtime, and Vanessa from fleet. We’ll keep it concrete.

[00:39] Derek Morrow: Great. I’ve got some graphs I can reference, but I’m assuming you’ve seen the same spikes.

[00:45] Aisha Bello: Yeah. We pulled the last 14 days for your dedicated pool in eu-west. We can’t see your prompts obviously, but we can see the request shapes and the runtime metrics. There’s a pattern.

[00:58] Priya Nair: Before we jump in, can I just set the context? Our primary endpoint is the “chat” style, max_new_tokens usually 256 to 512. Prompt varies, but we have a big chunk around, like, 1.5k tokens input.

[01:14] Noah Patel: That matches what we see in the distribution, yep.

[01:18] Marissa Cole: Derek, do you want to describe what you’re seeing from your side in terms of “what broke”?

[01:25] Derek Morrow: Sure. So historically, we had p95 under ~900 milliseconds for our “standard” call in eu-west. Last week we started seeing p95 jump to like 1.3 seconds during our peak, and p99 goes kind of nuts — like 3 to 5 seconds occasionally. It’s not constant, it comes and goes. Throughput also feels a bit lower, but it’s the tail that’s killing us.

[01:51] Aisha Bello: Yep. That’s consistent. The median is basically fine. p50 moved maybe, I don’t know, 5%? But p95 and p99 got worse in bursts.

[02:02] Lena Park: And we did not deploy anything on our side that should impact this. We’re not changing max tokens, no rollout, nothing. So, we’re suspecting infra or runtime change.

[02:14] Vanessa Ortiz: That’s fair. We did have an eu-west fleet adjustment — not a “new region” or anything, but a capacity rebalance. I’m still validating the exact timestamps, but it overlaps with your report window.

[02:28] Derek Morrow: Is that like GPU type change? Or driver? Because if it’s the same SKU, I’d expect more stability.

[02:35] Vanessa Ortiz: It’s a bit of both. Some of it is SKU mix during the rebalance, and there was also a driver patch that rolled through the pool. Again, I’m not going to claim causality before I send you the timeline.

[02:49] Noah Patel: Also, we had a scheduling heuristic tweak in the runtime around the same time, but it was supposed to be guarded. The thing is, we now have better signals to isolate whether the tail is queueing vs execution.

[03:04] Priya Nair: When you say scheduling tweak, you mean like batching and how you pack requests?

[03:09] Noah Patel: Exactly. Continuous batching, queue prioritization, and how we balance prefill-heavy requests vs decode-heavy requests.

[03:17] Aisha Bello: Let me share the breakdown in words. We see queueing time go up during the p95 spikes. Execution time (runtime-only) is comparatively stable. That points away from a kernel regression and more toward either the scheduler not keeping up under burst, or fewer effective GPUs, or fragmentation due to mixed workloads.

[03:40] Derek Morrow: That’s interesting because the customer impact aligns with our peak hour, which is like 17:00 to 20:00 CET.

[03:47] Aisha Bello: Yep — the spikes cluster in that window.

[03:51] Lena Park: So can you translate that into “what do we do”? Like do we need more dedicated capacity? Or do you fix the scheduling change?

[04:00] Marissa Cole: We’ll get to the mitigation options. But first, I want to be crisp on attribution so we don’t just throw GPUs at it if it’s a regression.

[04:10] Noah Patel: One more detail: batch size distribution shifted. During the window, we see smaller average batch sizes, which hurts tokens-per-second efficiency and can increase time-in-queue because you’re not draining the queue as effectively.

[04:26] Priya Nair: Smaller batch sizes could be because there’s more variability in request shapes, right?

[04:31] Noah Patel: Correct, or because the scheduler thresholds changed, or because the pool is underprovisioned and you’re getting more “micro-batches” due to pressure.

[04:41] Derek Morrow: We didn’t change our traffic mix. But… I guess end users are end users. Maybe the average prompt length drifted.

[04:48] Aisha Bello: We can check shape drift. We do store bucketed lengths, not content. And we can compare last week to the week before.

[04:56] Marissa Cole: Aisha, can you summarize what you saw there?

[05:00] Aisha Bello: There is a small shift toward longer prompts in the top bucket, but not enough to explain p99 going from ~2 seconds to 5 seconds. The bigger change is queueing time and the “inference slots” saturation.

[05:16] Vanessa Ortiz: Which is consistent with the fleet rebalance. If a portion of the pool was temporarily running at a different effective performance level, you can get that tail.

[05:27] Lena Park: Okay. So do you roll it back? Like, can you just revert whatever changed?

[05:33] Noah Patel: Two things. The runtime scheduling tweak already got partially rolled back for eu-west as of… I want to say Tuesday night. But I need to double check the exact commit that got disabled.

[05:46] Derek Morrow: That might explain why it felt “better” yesterday, but not fully fixed.

[05:51] Aisha Bello: Exactly. Yesterday p95 improved, but we still see occasional queue spikes.

[05:58] Marissa Cole: And the second thing is, we’re improving detection so we can catch this sort of regression before it hits you. That’s where the performance canary comes in.

[06:08] Priya Nair: Yeah, we saw mention of that in the email. How does that work? Is it like synthetic load?

[06:14] Noah Patel: Yeah. It’s a lightweight always-on canary that runs synthetic prompts against a set of models in production, per region. It measures end-to-end p95 and runtime-only p95, tokens per second, and splits like prefill vs decode vs queueing.

[06:30] Derek Morrow: Wait, so it hits the production inference endpoints? Doesn’t that affect capacity?

[06:35] Noah Patel: It does, but we cap it heavily. The target is under 0.5% GPU overhead per region for covered models. It’s basically a trickle, but enough samples to detect meaningful changes.

[06:48] Aisha Bello: And importantly, it doesn’t use customer prompts. It’s synthetic, fixed distributions, so privacy-wise it’s clean.

[06:56] Lena Park: And that canary would have caught this earlier?

[07:00] Noah Patel: It did catch a related issue during the rollout. We had a regression in another region where tokens/sec dropped after a kernel auto-selection change, and the canary flagged it within… I think 20 to 30 minutes, and we halted expansion.

[07:18] Marissa Cole: Also, we had some false positives early on — we can talk about that — but we improved baseline handling and anti-flap.

[07:26] Derek Morrow: I’m less worried about your internal process and more like, can we get a signal for our dedicated pool? Because we run dedicated to avoid this.

[07:35] Aisha Bello: Totally fair. Right now the canary is per model / per region, and dedicated pools can be included as a “tier.” We can enable warning-level notifications that include a dashboard link and the observed vs baseline.

[07:49] Priya Nair: Baseline relative to what? Like a fixed number or rolling?

[07:53] Noah Patel: It’s baseline artifacts computed per model, runtime version, and hardware SKU — and optionally per region. We generally use a rolling baseline with guardrails, because fixed baselines can get stale when fleet changes. But we also “pin” a baseline around releases so we can attribute.

[08:14] Derek Morrow: Rolling baseline scares me because if things get slowly worse you never alert.

[08:19] Aisha Bello: Yeah, that’s the tradeoff. We do a hybrid: rolling but bounded, and we have “freeze windows” around releases. We also enforce minimum sample size and a sustained window so you don’t page on noise.

[08:34] Marissa Cole: For your case, we can start with warning-only, no paging, and use it as an extra data point while we stabilize eu-west.

[08:43] Lena Park: That’s fine, but what about the current variance. What’s the plan for *fixing* it.

[08:49] Vanessa Ortiz: On the infra side, I can commit to sending the timeline today or tomorrow: when the SKU mix changed, and when the driver update rolled. If we see correlation, we can either standardize the pool back or adjust scheduling policies for that hardware.

[09:07] Noah Patel: On runtime, we want to validate whether queueing-time instrumentation is accurate in that pool and whether batch size distribution changed due to the scheduler tweak. If yes, we’ll keep the rollback in place and re-run the change behind a flag with canary gating.

[09:24] Derek Morrow: Can you share like a graph of queue time vs runtime time? Because right now we’re arguing internally whether it’s “slow GPUs” or “queue.”

[09:31] Aisha Bello: Yes. We have panels that break down end-to-end latency into queueing, prefill, decode. I’ll export a 14-day view and send it.

[09:42] Priya Nair: When you say “prefill,” that’s basically prompt processing, right?

[09:46] Noah Patel: Exactly. Prefill is the prompt tokens. Decode is generating the output tokens.

[09:52] Lena Park: Okay. And tokens-per-second, can you give that in a way we can compare to our internal expectations? Like per request or per GPU?

[10:00] Noah Patel: We generally report effective tokens/sec at the runtime level and also per request distribution. For a dedicated pool, we can provide an aggregate tokens/sec and “per concurrent slot” utilization.

[10:12] Derek Morrow: That would be useful, because we’ve been debating whether to increase our reservation.

[10:17] Marissa Cole: Let’s talk mitigation options. There are basically three levers: (1) stabilize the pool (remove variability), (2) tune autoscaling/queue thresholds so tail doesn’t explode, and (3) add headroom capacity if your peak is too close to saturation.

[10:34] Lena Park: We’d prefer (1) and (2) before we pay for (3), to be blunt.

[10:38] Marissa Cole: Completely reasonable.

[10:41] Aisha Bello: On (2), we can set stricter queue-time SLOs internally for your tier, so we alert before your p99 gets ugly. That’s more of an operational change than a product change.

[10:54] Derek Morrow: Is that what the canary does?

[10:56] Aisha Bello: The canary helps us detect runtime regressions. For queue-time, it’s also useful because it’s synthetic, so if queue time rises under constant canary load, it points to infra/scheduler rather than your traffic pattern. But it won’t replace real traffic monitoring. It complements.

[11:15] Priya Nair: I’m trying to understand something: if it’s a dedicated pool, why would queueing time change unless you changed something? Shouldn’t it be stable?

[11:24] Vanessa Ortiz: In a perfect world, yes. In reality, dedicated still has underlying fleet maintenance — like patching or moving capacity. We aim to do it with minimal disruption, but if the pool’s effective capacity drops temporarily, queue grows under the same demand.

[11:40] Derek Morrow: That’s basically what I suspected.

[11:43] Lena Park: So can we get a change management heads up? Like, “hey we’re patching eu-west dedicated”?

[11:49] Marissa Cole: For certain changes, yes. We can also align on a “maintenance window” expectation. Some of this was a capacity rebalance and should have been smoother; we can take that feedback.

[12:02] Aisha Bello: Also, we have been improving our incident-bot routing. When canary detects a sustained regression on a top model, it posts a thread with baseline vs observed, confidence, and direct runbook links. That speeds our rollback.

[12:17] Derek Morrow: Does that mean you’ll roll back faster next time?

[12:20] Noah Patel: That’s the goal. Before, we relied more on customer tickets or aggregate dashboards. Now we get an early warning per model/region, and it’s tied to runtime build tags and kernel version tags.

[12:36] Priya Nair: Kernel version tags? Like you can tell which kernel is selected?

[12:40] Noah Patel: Yeah, we attach a “kernel selection id” plus runtime build id into telemetry. So if you see p95 go up and the kernel id changed, you know where to look.

[12:52] Lena Park: That’s great, but again, we just want stable p95.

[12:56] Marissa Cole: Totally.

[12:58] Derek Morrow: I want to ask an uncomfortable question. We looked at AWS Bedrock as a fallback. We don’t want to move, but we can’t have customers seeing random 5 second responses.

[13:10] Marissa Cole: I appreciate you saying it directly. Dedicated is specifically for the stability you’re describing. Let’s treat this as a priority issue: stabilize eu-west, and add better early warning and comms.

[13:22] Aisha Bello: To be transparent, the last 48 hours are trending better after the scheduler rollback. The remaining tail spikes correlate with a subset of hosts. That’s why Vanessa’s timeline matters.

[13:36] Vanessa Ortiz: And we can isolate “bad actors” in the pool. If there’s a node group with worse performance, we can drain and replace.

[13:44] Priya Nair: Is it possible the model version changed? Like did you update weights or config?

[13:49] Noah Patel: For your pinned model, no weight changes in that window. There was a config change related to KV cache settings in another tier, but not yours.

[14:00] Derek Morrow: Okay.

[14:02] Marissa Cole: Can we align on what “good” means numerically for the next two weeks? Derek you said p95 < 900ms for your standard call. Is that still the target?

[14:11] Derek Morrow: Yeah. More precisely: p95 under 1 second for 256 output tokens, and p99 under 2.5 seconds. If p99 goes beyond 3 seconds we start seeing retries.

[14:25] Aisha Bello: That’s helpful. We can set internal warning thresholds around p95 and p99 deviations from baseline.

[14:33] Priya Nair: What’s the baseline right now? Because if you say “deviation,” and baseline is already degraded, it’s weird.

[14:38] Aisha Bello: Fair. For this, we’ll compute baseline from the “good window” prior to the incident — roughly early January. And we’ll annotate the graphs so it’s not drifting.

[14:52] Noah Patel: Also we can pin baseline by runtime version. So if we roll forward, we compare apples-to-apples.

[15:00] Derek Morrow: Okay, that’s what I want.

[15:02] Marissa Cole: Quick aside: we can share the dashboard link. It includes the queueing split. But we should be careful about access; it’s in our internal Grafana.

[15:10] Lena Park: Right, you can’t just give us your internal dashboard.

[15:13] Marissa Cole: Correct. What we can do is provide weekly exports and/or a customer-facing view in the console. The console work is in progress.

[15:24] Priya Nair: For now, a PDF or screenshot is fine. We mostly need confidence it’s under control.

[15:31] Aisha Bello: Understood.

[15:33] Noah Patel: Another question for you: do you have a top three “request shapes” list? Like prompt buckets and max_new_tokens distribution. It will help us tune canary profiles and the scheduler.

[15:45] Derek Morrow: We can provide a histogram. We already bucket prompt length. I can send you something like: 0–512, 512–1024, 1024–2048, >2048 and then output 128/256/512.

[15:59] Marissa Cole: Perfect.

[16:01] Lena Park: Going back to mitigation, what is the timeframe to stabilize eu-west? Days? Weeks?

[16:07] Vanessa Ortiz: For infra, days. If it’s a subset of nodes or a configuration mismatch, we can drain/replace quickly. If it’s a broader capacity constraint, that can also be addressed quickly, but it might require temporarily shifting capacity.

[16:22] Noah Patel: For runtime, the rollback is already in place. We’ll keep it until we can prove the new heuristic is safe via canary + staged load.

[16:32] Derek Morrow: That’s good. Please don’t re-enable without telling us.

[16:36] Marissa Cole: Agreed. We’ll coordinate.

[16:39] Aisha Bello: And to your earlier question about “why didn’t you see this earlier,” the honest answer is: we had monitoring, but it wasn’t per-model and it didn’t have great attribution. The canary is closing that gap.

[16:54] Priya Nair: Did you have an incident last week? Like internal?

[16:58] Aisha Bello: We didn’t declare a Sev incident because it didn’t cross global thresholds, but for you it absolutely mattered. We should have treated dedicated pool variance as a customer-impact incident. That’s on us.

[17:12] Lena Park: Thanks for saying that.

[17:14] Marissa Cole: We’ll do better.

[17:16] Derek Morrow: Okay. On alerts: can we get something in Slack? Like a heads up when you see p95 regression.

[17:23] Aisha Bello: We can route warning-level canary alerts to a shared Slack Connect channel if you have one with us. It would be limited info: model, region, observed vs baseline, and a link to a status note. No internals.

[17:39] Lena Park: That’s fine. We have Slack Connect with your support team.

[17:42] Marissa Cole: Great. We’ll coordinate with support to add the right folks.

[17:48] Priya Nair: Question: would those alerts trigger often? I don’t want noise.

[17:53] Noah Patel: We have anti-flap: minimum samples and sustained window. Also dedupe. Early on we had an alert storm because of baseline drift and label cardinality issues. We fixed the label set and dampening.

[18:10] Derek Morrow: Label cardinality issues… that sounds like a Prometheus thing.

[18:14] Aisha Bello: Exactly. Too many dimensions, baseline computed wrong, lots of false positives. Now it’s constrained: model id, model version, region, hardware SKU, runtime build. That’s it.

[18:29] Lena Park: Okay.

[18:31] Marissa Cole: I want to make sure we answer your biggest question: “Do we need more reserved capacity?” What do you think, Derek, based on what you’re seeing? Are you saturating?

[18:41] Derek Morrow: Hard to say. We’re close to the line during peak. But before this, it was fine. So I’m reluctant to blame demand.

[18:51] Aisha Bello: From our view, you are running hot during peak — not pegged 100% all the time, but there’s less headroom than I’d like for tail stability. That said, the sudden change indicates something shifted on our side.

[19:09] Vanessa Ortiz: One possibility is during the rebalance, effective headroom temporarily reduced. So even if your normal reservation is okay, you see tail if we’re at lower effective capacity.

[19:22] Priya Nair: If you fix that, do we still need more capacity?

[19:25] Marissa Cole: Let’s re-evaluate after we stabilize. If you want, we can do a short load test off-peak to quantify headroom. But I don’t want to distract from the immediate fix.

[19:36] Lena Park: Agreed.

[19:38] Derek Morrow: Can you also confirm no multi-tenancy? Like we’re not sharing GPUs.

[19:42] Marissa Cole: Correct. Your dedicated pool is isolated capacity. The control plane and some telemetry infra is shared, but the GPU workers are dedicated.

[19:53] Derek Morrow: Good.

[19:55] Noah Patel: One more helpful detail: we can expose “queue depth” and “batch size distribution” trendlines in the report. That’ll make it clearer whether it’s queueing.

[20:06] Priya Nair: That would help us explain to product.

[20:10] Marissa Cole: Okay, so here’s what I’m hearing as the plan: Aisha sends the 14-day report with splits. Vanessa sends infra timeline and what changed in eu-west. Noah enables warning-level canary monitoring for your model in eu-west and shares how it’ll be communicated. Derek sends request shape histogram. Then we meet in two weeks.

[20:30] Lena Park: Yes. But I also want an explicit commitment on “no re-enable of the scheduler change without canary gating.”

[20:37] Noah Patel: Agreed. We’re moving toward gating runtime rollouts with canary signals, especially for top models and dedicated tiers. For eu-west, we can keep the feature flag off until we have clean canary runs.

[20:53] Derek Morrow: Great.

[20:55] Aisha Bello: Also, for completeness: if the variance returns in the next few days, we’ll treat it as a customer-impact incident and loop in on-call earlier. That’s a process change we’re making.

[21:07] Lena Park: Thank you.

[21:09] Priya Nair: Can I ask one more question about tokens-per-second? Because we did notice throughput seemed lower.

[21:16] Noah Patel: Sure.

[21:17] Priya Nair: Is it possible the KV cache hit rate changed? Like are we getting less reuse?

[21:22] Noah Patel: In general, KV cache hit rate is workload-dependent. We don’t cache across customers, and within a dedicated pool, caching depends on repeated prefixes. For chat, unless you have repeated system prompts, it’s limited. That said, we’re considering adding KV cache hit-rate as a canary metric for attribution, but it’s not a main driver for your case.

[21:45] Derek Morrow: Our system prompt is stable but user messages vary. So yeah, not much reuse.

[21:51] Noah Patel: Right. The throughput drop we saw aligns more with smaller batch sizes and more time spent waiting. Effective tokens/sec goes down when you’re underutilizing the GPU.

[22:05] Priya Nair: Makes sense.

[22:07] Vanessa Ortiz: Also if the pool has mixed SKU temporarily, tokens/sec can appear lower if slower hosts are serving more.

[22:15] Marissa Cole: We’ll quantify it in the report.

[22:18] Derek Morrow: Cool.

[22:20] (cross talk)

[22:21] Lena Park: Sorry, go ahead Derek.

[22:23] Derek Morrow: Just to be clear, we’re not asking for a bunch of custom work. We just need stability, and visibility when something changes.

[22:31] Marissa Cole: Totally. And this is aligned with what we’re building anyway.

[22:36] Aisha Bello: One more thing: we can also provide a “change log” view for the pool — runtime build id changes, kernel selection changes, fleet changes. It’s internal today, but we can summarize it in the weekly email.

[22:51] Lena Park: That would be huge.

[22:54] Marissa Cole: Great. Let’s do that.

[22:57] Derek Morrow: When do you think you can send the first report?

[23:00] Aisha Bello: I can send an initial cut by Friday end of day UTC, so tomorrow. It might be a little rough, but it’ll have the splits and the main windows highlighted.

[23:12] Derek Morrow: Perfect.

[23:14] Marissa Cole: Vanessa, timeline?

[23:16] Vanessa Ortiz: Same. I’ll confirm with infra logs and send the timestamps of fleet changes by Saturday latest.

[23:23] Lena Park: Okay.

[23:25] Noah Patel: And I’ll coordinate with Aisha on enabling the canary warnings for your region/model. We’ll keep it “warn only” until we’re confident.

[23:35] Priya Nair: Great.

[23:37] Marissa Cole: I think we can wrap early unless there are other questions.

[23:41] Lena Park: I have one more. If this happens again, what’s the escalation path? Support ticket feels too slow.

[23:48] Marissa Cole: For dedicated, you should open a Sev2 with support, but we’ll also route it to our on-call directly. We’ll share the escalation matrix in the follow-up email. Aisha can include it.

[24:02] Aisha Bello: Yep, I’ll include “who to page” and what info helps: region, approximate window, and whether it’s p95/p99 or throughput.

[24:12] Derek Morrow: Cool.

[24:14] Priya Nair: And can you confirm you don’t store prompts in canary or metrics? Our security folks will ask.

[24:20] Noah Patel: Confirmed. Canary uses synthetic prompts generated internally. For metrics, we store only bucketed lengths and aggregate histograms, no prompt text.

[24:32] Priya Nair: Great.

[24:34] Marissa Cole: Alright. Thanks everyone. We’ll send the recap with next steps and dates.

[24:40] Lena Park: Thanks.

[24:41] Derek Morrow: Thank you.

[24:42] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[24:44] Meeting ended.

Note: Fireflies timestamping can be approximate; some crosstalk may be misattributed.
